clue.text: I'm unfortunately suffering setback — it must be the sausage

indicators.note: a setback sends things the wrong way, so the opening words are read from the end back to the start

parts.note: alas is the cry of regret, meaning unfortunately

explanation.surface: Someone blames their bad luck on what they ate: the sausage must be to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' reads as a comment on the speaker's luck, but it supplies a word of regret, and the setback turns both opening words round together.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a highly seasoned Italian cured sausage, usually eaten sliced and cold.

clue.text: Iron block found in Russian village

indicators.note: the answer is literally located inside the run of letters that follows

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A lump of iron is discovered in a remote Russian settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: An anvil is the heavy iron block on which a smith hammers metal.

clue.text: Correspondence emissary brought over about me returning

indicators.note: brought over something means placed around it, so the outer word encloses the rest

parts.note: an agent is someone sent on another's behalf

indicators.note: something returning goes back the way it came, so that word is read right to left

explanation.surface: A diplomat ferries over letters concerning the writer, who is coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correspondence' tempts you toward letters and post; here it means matching, and the emissary wraps both short pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Correspondence in the sense of matching or harmony is a synonym for agreement.

clue.text: One so overdue has to be cut off

explanation.surface: Someone who has failed to pay a bill on time has their supply disconnected.
explanation.definitionFit: To isolate something is to separate it, so the verb is synonymous with cut off.

clue.text: Stupid being blunt

definitions.meaning: second meaning: not sharp or pointed

explanation.surface: Someone is called dim for speaking too frankly.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both dull wit and a rounded, unpointed shape, as in an angle over ninety degrees.

clue.text: Oscar, or band playing in support?

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: letters that are playing move about freely rather than staying in line

explanation.surface: Is it a film award or a group performing as the support act?
explanation.definitionFit: To be on board with a plan is an idiom for backing it, so the phrase means supportive.

clue.text: I chewed up a bone

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: bit is a past tense of bite, close to chewed

explanation.surface: A dog's confession: I gnawed a bone to pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The tibia is the shinbone, the larger of the two bones in the lower leg.

clue.text: Lawyer is cool — writ amended without hint of worry

indicators.note: a document that is amended has been altered, so the letters are set in a new order
the hint of a word is its opening letter, and without says that letter is dropped from the writ

parts.note: taken as written, before its first letter goes

explanation.surface: A lawyer stays calm as a legal writ is redrafted, without any concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool' looks like the lawyer's calm manner, but it is plain fodder; the hint of worry is its opening letter, removed before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a solicitor is the kind of lawyer who advises clients and prepares cases, as opposed to a barrister.

clue.text: Tigris and Euphrates, for the record

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the two great rivers of ancient Mesopotamia
second meaning: a 1978 hit single by Boney M

explanation.surface: A geography note naming two rivers, 'for the record'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For the record' looks like an idiom meaning officially; it actually points to a pop song of that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Babylon stood on the Euphrates near the Tigris, and the phrase also names a famous Boney M single drawn from Psalm 137.

clue.text: Scottish poet depicting Welsh actress, Rachel, crossing stream

indicators.note: the actress's name spans across the stream, holding it in its middle

parts.note: Rachel Roberts was a Welsh film and stage actress
burn is the Scottish word for a stream

explanation.surface: A painting of a Welsh actress wading over a brook supposedly shows a Scottish poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns, author of Auld Lang Syne, is Scotland's national poet.

clue.text: Cleaned them out for a local derby, perhaps

indicators.note: turned out of their places, the letters must be set in a new order

explanation.surface: A team thrashes its rivals in a derby against neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: A local derby is a game between two teams from the same town.
explanation.definitionFit: A needle match is a fixture with intense personal rivalry, and a derby between neighbouring clubs is a typical example.

clue.text: Rubbish may be left in large crate at the far end

indicators.note: one item sits inside the other word

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left

indicators.note: the far end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Junk might be abandoned at the back of a big packing case.
explanation.definitionFit: Bilge is the foul water in a ship's hull, and by extension a slang word for nonsense.

clue.text: Runs from large farm in a valley in flood

indicators.note: one part is placed within the other
taking one thing from another removes it

parts.note: R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for runs
a ranch is a large farm

explanation.surface: Water pours off a big farm as a valley floods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like the verb for water flowing; it is the cricket abbreviation, taken away from the farm.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively an avalanche is an overwhelming deluge of things, much as a flood of letters or complaints.

clue.text: Full? New peer's allowed inside

indicators.note: the second part goes inside the first
a new version of a word has its letters made over

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged; the 's is read as 'has'

explanation.surface: Is the House of Lords full now that a newly created lord has been admitted?
explanation.definitionFit: Replete means filled to capacity, especially well fed, so it is a synonym of full.

clue.text: Tradesman dressing emergency room

parts.note: a plaster is a sticking dressing for a wound
ER is the abbreviation for emergency room

explanation.surface: A workman is having a wound dressed in casualty.
explanation.definitionFit: A plasterer is a skilled building worker who coats walls and ceilings, one of the trades.

clue.text: Key drug is not available

indicators.note: something not available is absent, so those letters are removed

parts.note: digitalis is a heart drug made from foxgloves

explanation.surface: A vital medicine is out of stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key' looks like an adjective meaning crucial; it is a noun here, a key of a keyboard instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: In Chambers a digital is also a noun for a key played by the finger, as on a piano or organ.

clue.text: Magnificent farceur keeping quiet in film

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the soft-music letter is held within

parts.note: Brian Rix was a British actor famous for Whitehall farces
p (piano) is the musical marking for quiet

explanation.surface: A splendid comic actor stays silent in a movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Grand Prix is a 1966 John Frankenheimer motor-racing film.

clue.text: Lucky dip bishop organised on boat

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to run an event is to organise it
a tub is a slow, clumsy boat; 'on' just places it after

explanation.surface: A clergyman arranges a prize draw aboard ship.
explanation.walkthrough: A bran tub is a British fete game: a tub of bran with small prizes buried in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A bran tub is a lucky dip, a barrel you reach into to pull out a hidden prize.

clue.text: First to eat in remarkable nearby restaurant that's cheap

indicators.note: remarkable here means worth re-marking, letters set out anew in another order
the first of the next word is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A recommendation for a striking cheap café close at hand where you should eat first.
explanation.definitionFit: Beanery is American slang for a cheap eating house, so it fits a low-cost restaurant.

clue.text: Snide remark about a zodiac sign in chart

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the remark wraps around the next item

parts.note: a dig is a sly jibe

explanation.surface: Someone makes a sneering comment about a star sign on a horoscope chart.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a drawing or plan that sets out information visually, much like a chart.

clue.text: French army officer wants short fuse attached to nest

indicators.note: a word that is short has been cut, losing its last letter

parts.note: a drey is a squirrel's nest

explanation.surface: An explosives officer needs a shorter fuse fixed to a nest.
explanation.walkthrough: A drey is the nest a squirrel builds of twigs high in a tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Dreyfus was the French artillery captain wrongly convicted of treason in the Dreyfus affair.

clue.text: Fight back at atelier resolved

indicators.note: resolved suggests something broken down and put together again, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An artist decides to strike back in the studio.
explanation.walkthrough: An atelier is an artist's workshop.
explanation.definitionFit: To retaliate is to respond to an attack with a counter-attack, which is fighting back.

clue.text: Nobody's child?

parts.note: surface reading: an orphan or foundling, a child belonging to no one
setter's reading: the son of Charles Pooter in the Grossmiths' novel The Diary of a Nobody

explanation.walkthrough: Capitalised at the start, 'Nobody' hides the title character of The Diary of a Nobody.
explanation.definitionFit: Lupin Pooter is the son of the diarist Charles Pooter, the 'Nobody' of the comic novel.

clue.text: Went via the underground, returned in launch

indicators.note: something returned goes back where it came from, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: the Tube is London's underground railway, so travelling on it is to tube

explanation.surface: Someone took the Underground home for a product launch.
explanation.definitionFit: A debut is a first public appearance, the launch of a performer or product.

clue.text: Hired assassin's code word

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a hired ruffian or killer; the 's reads as 'is'
second meaning: the NATO phonetic alphabet word for B

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a hitman's secret password; the two halves are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Bravo is an old word for a hired cut-throat, and it is also the radio code word for the letter B.

clue.text: Maltreated pets of card sharp short of money

indicators.note: something maltreated has been knocked about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A broke cheat at cards has been mistreating the animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Strapped for cash is an informal idiom for being hard up, lacking funds.

clue.text: Spirit's label beginning to yellow

parts.note: a brand is a trade name or label

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is just its first letter

explanation.surface: The label on a bottle of liquor is starting to go yellow with age.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandy is a spirit distilled from wine, one example of strong liquor.

clue.text: Grave-digger attacked, about ten

indicators.note: about means round, so the first part surrounds the second

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten

explanation.surface: A cemetery worker was assaulted at around ten o'clock.
explanation.definitionFit: A sexton is a church officer whose duties traditionally include digging graves.
